A hash table stores key-value pairs in an array of slots called buckets. Its purpose is to answer a question such as "what value belongs to this key?" without examining every key. The central trick is the hash function, which transforms a key into a number. The table uses that number, usually reduced modulo the number of buckets, to choose a bucket. A lookup begins at that chosen bucket rather than at the beginning of the whole collection. This is why hash tables are common in dictionaries, symbol tables, caches, and database indexes: when the arrangements are good, a lookup jumps almost directly to the right neighborhood.

A hash function is a deterministic procedure that accepts a key and returns an integer. The same key must produce the same result while the table is unchanged, or a later lookup would not know where to go. A good hash function is fast and spreads keys as evenly as possible across the bucket numbers. It is not normally an encryption function and does not need to be reversible; its practical job is to distribute keys. Because there are only finitely many buckets and far more possible keys, different keys will sometimes map to the same bucket. Such an event is a collision, and no useful hash function can eliminate collisions entirely; it can only make them less common and less predictable for ordinary data.

Chaining handles collisions by allowing one bucket to hold more than one entry. Each bucket is associated with a chain of entries that hash to it. Every entry stores the full key, the associated value, and a link to the next entry. To find a value, the table hashes the search key, goes to the indicated bucket, and walks along its chain. At each entry it compares the stored key with the search key. If the keys are equal, the lookup returns that entry's value. If the chain ends without an equal key, the table reports that the key is absent. Comparing keys, rather than bucket numbers, is essential: two different keys can land in the same bucket, so arriving there proves only that a key might be present.

A small invented example makes the process concrete. Imagine five buckets numbered zero through four. For this illustration only, not as any real hash function, suppose cedar is assigned to bucket two, maple to bucket four, and pine also to bucket two. Pine and cedar form a two-entry chain in bucket two, while maple sits alone in bucket four. Suppose cedar stores "fragrant evergreen," maple "sweet wood," and pine "coniferous tree." To look up pine, the table applies the same made-up rule and lands on bucket two. It examines cedar, sees that the keys differ, follows the link to pine, and finds a match, returning "coniferous tree." Looking up maple goes directly to bucket four and finds its sole entry. A lookup for an absent key that hashed to bucket two would examine cedar and pine, reach the end of the chain, and conclude the key was absent.

The cost of such a search depends heavily on how long the chains are. A useful measure is the load factor, usually the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. With chaining, the load factor can exceed one, because a bucket may hold several entries. If the load factor is low, chains tend to be short, and lookups require few comparisons. If it climbs, buckets become crowded and lookups take longer. To prevent this, an implementation monitors the load factor and resizes when it crosses a threshold. Resizing means allocating a larger bucket array and then reinserting every existing entry according to the new number of buckets. Entries usually cannot simply be copied into the same bucket numbers, because reducing a hash value modulo a different bucket count generally changes the result. Rehashing every entry takes time proportional to the number of entries, but it happens only occasionally, so its cost can be spread across many insertions. After resizing, the load factor falls, chains shorten, and lookup performance improves again.

Under favorable conditions, lookup is expected to take constant time, written as O(1). This does not mean every lookup takes exactly the same number of operations. It means that, averaged over ordinary keys and a well-distributed hash function, the work is bounded by a constant plus a term proportional to the load factor. If the table keeps that factor bounded, the average chain length is constant, so the number of entries examined is constant on average. A particular lookup can still be slower because its key shares a bucket with several others. The worst case is different: if all n keys collide in one bucket, that chain has n entries, and finding an entry near the end or proving absence may require examining all n. A lookup then takes linear time, O(n), because the table has degenerated into a linked list. A poor hash function, badly distributed data, or an adversary deliberately choosing colliding keys can cause this. Randomizing the hash function can make such an attack harder, but it cannot prevent all bad consequences. Thus the familiar constant-time reputation is an expected-case guarantee under good hashing and controlled load, while the worst case remains linear when collisions overwhelm the distribution.

In practice, a well-built hash table uses a fast, evenly spreading hash function, keeps the load factor sensible, and resizes by rehashing when needed. These choices make long chains unlikely, so most lookups perform a hash calculation, one bucket access, and a few key comparisons. It trades extra space and occasional rehashing work for finding most values by jumping to a narrow set of candidates. That is how the lookup finds its way.

"Under favorable conditions, lookup is expected to take constant time, written as O(1). This does not mean every lookup takes exactly the same number of operations. It means that, averaged over ordinary keys and a well-distributed hash function, the work is bounded by a constant plus a term proportional to the load factor. A poor hash function, badly distributed data, or an adversary who deliberately chooses colliding keys can cause this. A randomized hash function can make such an attack harder, but it cannot prevent collisions from having bad consequences. Thus the familiar constant-time reputation of hash tables is an expected-case guarantee under good hashing and controlled load, while the worst case remains linear when collisions overwhelm the distribution."
